# Analysis of 10. Bb5

You've moved your bishop to b5 to pin Black's knight on c6, but this move doesn't accomplish anything concrete right now. Black can simply play **...a6**, forcing your bishop to make a decision without having improved White's position. You've also moved away from where your bishop can be more useful.

Instead, play **Ba2**. This move prepares to support your center and keeps your bishop on the long diagonal pointing at g8, where it eyes Black's kingside. More importantly, Ba2 gets your bishop out of the way so you can develop smoothly with moves like Nc3 or castle kingside without the bishop becoming a target. It's a quiet developing move that improves your position without giving Black any free tempo-gaining opportunities like ...a6.

The key principle: don't make your opponent react to threats they can easily parry. Instead, develop your pieces to squares where they're naturally well-placed and support your plan.

More critically, it ignores that Black's bishop on c8 and queen on d8 are eyeing your kingside, and your knight on e2 is awkwardly placed.

**What you should play instead:**

Play **Ng3** to accomplish two things: First, you move your knight to a more active square where it defends h1 and supports your f4 pawn. Second—and this is the key tactical point—you prepare to reroute your knight to h5 or f5 later, putting real pressure on Black's kingside. Right now your knight on e2 isn't contributing to your attack, so improving its placement with tempo (threatening ideas on the kingside) is much more forcing than a quiet pawn push.

Here, d4 pushes your pawn but leaves e2 undefended—that's a classic setup for a fork or a simple capture. Play **Ng3 instead**: it's active, it's solid, and it doesn't gift material away.

After Black plays Bxf3, you have to recapture (probably with your bishop on d2), but this trades away your active pieces and leaves Black with a safer position. The engine prefers **Qf2** because it keeps your queen on the second rank where it's protected by your rook on f1—Black's bishop can't threaten it there. By playing Qf2, you maintain the same control and pressure on Black's position without hanging your queen to a free capture. Always check if your opponent's pieces can snap up your queen before you move it to an "active" square.

explanations.haiku:
# Why gxh5 was a mistake

You've traded away your last active pawn while your king is poorly placed to support the endgame. After gxh5, Black plays Bf8 and then pushes g5, and your king on g3 can't stop both the g-pawn and support your queenside pawns—Black's bishop and king work together to pick off your queenside while the g-pawn advances.

**You should have played Kh4 instead.** This move activates your king toward Black's kingside pawns and threatens to capture on h5 yourself. After Kh4, if Black plays hxg4, you recapture with hxg4, and now you have a passed g-pawn while your king is actively attacking Black's remaining pawns. Your king becomes a real threat in the race, which you lose with the passive gxh5.

The key difference: Kh4 keeps your g-pawn alive as a weapon and gets your king involved in the fight; gxh5 eliminates your pawn advantage and leaves your king stranded on g3 with no winning prospects.
explanations.haiku+sae:

After gxh5, Black plays hxg4, and you've traded away your dangerous passed g-pawn without making progress. Your king on g3 then has to deal with Black's counterplay on the queenside while the position stays messy.

Instead, play **Kh4**. This move does two critical things: it attacks Black's h5 pawn directly, *forcing* Black to respond to the threat rather than create their own. After Black plays hxg4 (or loses the h5 pawn), you recapture hxg4, and now your h-pawn becomes the passed pawn while Black's bishop on g7 is too far away to stop it. You're winning because your king is actively attacking, not reacting.

The key lesson: **don't trade pawns when you can improve your king first**. Move your king to where it threatens something, and only trade when your opponent is forced to respond to *your* threats, not the other way around.
